sources.title: The Paradox of Suspense

discussion.body: The sting of the account is that fear here is aimed at something that may never happen. The emotion is doing its work on a merely possible event, which is why it can be manufactured before anything goes wrong.

It also makes tension a dial rather than a mood. Raise the danger or the odds of the bad outcome and the fear is supposed to rise with them, which is a claim you can test by rewriting the same scene with worse stakes.
Fine, but on this account dread alone is not suspense. You also need hope in the mix — something the viewer wants to happen — or you have atmosphere rather than a scene that pulls.

items.title: Fear, Hope, and Not Knowing: The Recipe Suspense Runs On
items.body: Cognitive psychologists Ortony, Clore, and Collins describe suspense as a compound of three ingredients: fear, hope, and uncertainty. As the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy lays out their account, fear is displeasure about the prospect of an undesirable event, hope is pleasure about the prospect of a desirable one, and suspense shows up when both are running and the outcome is genuinely unsettled. People feel suspense, on this view, when they fear a bad outcome, hope for a good one, and do not know which will arrive. Think of that as a working definition for a tense scene, not just a mood word for a tense viewer. The encyclopedia's analogy is everyday rather than cinematic: walking at night through an unfamiliar neighborhood you have heard is dangerous, fearing a mugging, hoping to arrive safe, uncertain which way it goes. What makes the account useful is that they treat fear and hope as prospect emotions — feelings aimed at an outcome that has not been decided yet. Their intensity is not arbitrary. It tracks two variables: how desirable or undesirable the outcome would be, and how likely it is. Fear, in their telling, grows as the danger worsens, the outcome gets worse, or the odds of it happening rise.

sources.title: Public Goods

items.title: Rice Is Rivalrous; Bruckner Is Not
items.body: Paul Samuelson is usually credited with bringing the theory of public goods into modern economics, but the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy notes the idea predates him, reaching back to John Stuart Mill, the Italian public-finance writer Ugo Mazzola, and the Swedish economist Knut Wicksell. Samuelson's own term was a mouthful: he defined a collective consumption good as one that all enjoy in common, in the sense that each individual's consumption of it leads to no subtraction from anyone else's consumption of the same good. Contemporary economics has a tidier label for that feature: non-rivalry. The definition runs on subtraction rather than popularity. A good is rivalrous exactly when one person's consumption diminishes someone else's ability to consume it. The encyclopedia's two examples do the work better than a definition can. Bob's consumption of a grain of rice makes it impossible for Sally to consume that same grain — the object is used up, so rice is rivalrous. Sally's enjoyment of Bruckner's Symphony No. 9, by contrast, does not diminish Bob's ability to enjoy it. Rice is consumed once; one person enjoying the symphony does not use up another person's opportunity to enjoy it.

sources.title: GlobalEye surveillance plane under the microscope as Conservatives call for twin probes

items.title: Conservatives Want Audits of Ottawa's GlobalEye Purchase
items.body: CBC reports that the federal Conservatives want the auditor general and the parliamentary budget officer to investigate Ottawa's planned GlobalEye purchase, questioning whether proper procurement rules were followed. The demand follows reporting that the Saab aircraft meets only some military requirements, and that competitors had not been shown those requirements before the government announced its preferred aircraft. The request seeks scrutiny of the procurement process. What the complaint targets, at least on its face, is the sequence: requirements that competing bidders did not see before a preferred aircraft was named.

sources.title: FCC lets Paramount sell 49.5% equity stake to Saudi Arabia, UAE, and Qatar

discussion.body: Two separate gates are visible here: the FCC signed off on the foreign ownership stakes, while the merger itself sits contested in court and separately approved by the Justice Department.

Separate on paper, but the financing is the link. The deal is partly financed by foreign investment, so clearing the ownership question looks like progress toward closing a merger that states are still trying to stop.

items.title: FCC Clears Sovereign-Fund Stakes That Take Paramount's Foreign Ownership to 49.5%
items.body: The Federal Communications Commission approved Paramount Skydance's plan to sell large equity stakes to the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, and Qatar, Ars Technica reports. Under US law, companies holding broadcast licenses need FCC approval for direct or indirect foreign ownership above 25 percent of their stock. Paramount says its indirect foreign ownership will reach 49.5 percent once the sovereign fund investments land, and it petitioned the FCC to waive the limit. The stakes matter because of what Paramount owns: the company holds licenses for the 28 local CBS stations it owns and operates. The approval does not settle the larger deal it is attached to. Paramount is buying Warner Bros. Discovery in a $111 billion transaction that is partially financed with foreign investment, and the acquisition has not closed because US states filed a lawsuit aiming to block the merger. The Department of Justice approved that merger.

sources.title: NASA Invites Media to Albania Artemis Accords Signing Ceremony

items.title: Albania Set to Become the 73rd Country to Sign the Artemis Accords
items.body: Albania will sign the Artemis Accords during a ceremony at noon EDT on Monday, Sept. 21, at NASA Headquarters in Washington, becoming the 73rd country signatory. NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson is set to host Albania's minister for Europe and foreign affairs, Ferit Hoxha, and its ambassador to the United States, Ervin Bushati, for the signing, alongside State Department officials. The event is in person only, with media required to RSVP in advance. The Accords introduced the first set of practical principles aimed at enhancing the safety, transparency and coordination of civil space exploration on the Moon.

sources.title: Finding the cells that put our brain to sleep

discussion.body: A one-percent population of inhibitory neurons acting as a sleep switch is a strikingly small lever for such a large behavior.
The claim is narrower than that. It is about the cortex initiating the rhythm, not about these cells running the whole sleep system.

items.title: A Small Group of Inhibitory Neurons Can Send a Mouse to Sleep
items.body: Somewhere in the cortex sits a small population of cells that can put a mouse to sleep. In a recent Nature study, neuroscientist Geoffrey Terral and Renata Batista-Brito, who runs the lab, report that these cells make up only around one percent of the cortex's inhibitory neurons, and that switching them on sends the animal to sleep. The claim is about initiation, not mere response. The study's argument is that the cortex can not only register the slow rhythm of deep sleep but also start it on its own — and that this is sufficient to promote sleep.

sources.title: How Cambodian Pop Music Survived the Khmer Rouge

discussion.body: Ethnographer Stephen Mamula, conducting fieldwork in Phnom Penh between 2004 and 2006, was struck by the musical vitality of the country's soundscape and the ubiquity of colorful CD jewel cases on display. He found that access to technologies such as television and compact discs was instrumental in regenerating indigenous culture.
That puts the return in an unexpected place: consumer hardware, TV sets and discs, as the vehicle that carried a tradition back into daily life.

items.title: The Khmer Rouge Killed Nine in Ten of Cambodia's Professional Musicians. The Music Came Back.
items.body: Under the Khmer Rouge regime of the 1970s, Cambodia's entertainment venues were shuttered and nine in ten of the country's professional musicians were killed. Cambodia's popular music culture then virtually ceased to exist for a twenty-year period — and, against the odds, has since made a remarkable comeback.

sources.title: Trump says he's banning 3 outlets from White House in his latest attack on press freedom

items.title: Trump Says He Is Barring CNN, MS NOW and Politico From the White House
items.body: President Donald Trump says he is banning three major news outlets — CNN, MS NOW and Politico — from the White House, citing what he called “unfavorable coverage.” He did not provide details on how the ban would be implemented, and warned that he might bar other media outlets as well.

sources.title: Deploy Hugging Face models on Amazon SageMaker AI with coding agents

discussion.body: The telling phrase is "quietly wrong." Getting an endpoint to run is not the same as making sound deployment decisions; that is the risk AWS says the skills are meant to address.
Skills still encode the decisions someone thought to write down. The current container tag for a particular region is exactly the kind of detail that may need updating.
They also claim a verified teardown path. An endpoint you can start is only half the story; the workflow promises a way to shut it down, too.

items.title: Attach the skills, don't let the agent improvise
items.body:
The pitch for coding agents is that you describe what you want — a model running behind a real-time endpoint, say — walk away, and come back to a working deployment. AWS's own write-up on deploying Hugging Face models with SageMaker AI names the failure mode directly: an unguided agent "might make wrong decisions, producing endpoints that are fragile, costly, or quietly wrong."

The problem is worst with new models, because the agent's training data may not contain the deployment knowledge the task requires — the right serving container for a given architecture, the current image tag for a specific AWS Region, an instance type matched to the model's memory footprint, autoscaling that doesn't burn GPU hours on an idle endpoint, alarms that catch silent failures.

The proposed fix is narrower than "better prompting": install six pre-written skills from Hugging Face Skills and point the agent at them. AWS describes the agent producing an endpoint with autoscaling, CloudWatch alarms, the correct container from the AWS Deep Learning Containers catalog, and a verified teardown path.

That's a real engineering tradeoff, not just a product announcement. You're outsourcing the agent's deployment judgment to a curated skill set rather than hoping general competence covers a task where being quietly wrong is the expensive outcome.

sources.title: Asteroids

discussion.body: The Moon comparison gives the population a scale; Vesta gives one member a scale. Keeping those two measurements separate makes the contrast more useful.
The size range is also doing work: Vesta at roughly 530 kilometers versus sub-10-meter bodies means "asteroid" spans objects that are worlds and objects that are boulders.

items.title: All the Asteroids Together Weigh Less Than the Moon
items.body:
NASA describes asteroids as rocky, airless remnants of the solar system's formation about 4.6 billion years ago. Most orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter in the main asteroid belt.

The size range is striking: Vesta is about 530 kilometers across, while some asteroids are smaller than 10 meters. Yet NASA puts the combined mass of all asteroids below that of Earth's Moon.

The contrast is between the size of an individual object and the mass of the whole population. A body hundreds of kilometers across can belong to a population whose total mass is still less than the Moon's.

sources.title: The Women Written Out of Mining History

discussion.body: Calling these laws protective casts exclusion as care. The scholars' account makes that language difficult to separate from the loss of women's visibility in mining history.
The household framing matters: if early modern mining involved the whole family, its later masculine image cannot simply be treated as a timeless description of the work.

items.title: The eviction that got written out of mining history
items.body:
The stock image of a miner — the brawny figure at the coal face, the gold-rush prospector — is about as masculine as an occupational stereotype gets. According to scholars Rossana Barragán Romano and Leda Papastefanaki, women have mined around the world throughout history, and early modern mining was a household affair in which every member of a family took on mining tasks. Women, they write, "were as active as miners in the past as they are in the present."

They also give a mechanism for the discrepancy. Mining came to be considered — and legislated — as men's work, which they argue largely erased women from its recorded history. Over two centuries, women were evicted from European and North American mines as "protective" laws barred them from working in them.

The erasure has a present-tense cost. Today, in some countries, women can make up as much as half of the millions of people working in artisanal and small-scale mining, the sector the UN and World Bank call ASM — work the scholars describe as often taking place under the worst and most precarious conditions. That makes this more than a question about the archive: it also concerns whose work gets noticed in the present.

sources.title: GDPNow Goes Gangbusters

items.title: GDP Growth Rates Need Their Time Periods Attached
items.body:
Econbrowser reports an Atlanta Fed GDPNow estimate of 5.1 percent annualized quarter-over-quarter growth for the third quarter. In the same post, the FT-Booth forecast is 2 percent fourth-quarter-over-fourth-quarter growth.

Those labels matter. The first describes a quarter's growth expressed at an annual rate; the second compares the fourth quarter with the fourth quarter a year earlier. They are not two directly comparable estimates of the same span.

Econbrowser also places GDPNow above the other nowcasts it charts. That reported disagreement is worth distinguishing from the tempting 5.1-versus-2 comparison: before treating a gap as a dispute about the economy, check that both numbers measure growth over the same period.

sources.title: U.S.-Saudi nuclear power deal faces pushback over potential weapons risks

items.title: Democrats Move to Block a U.S.-Saudi Civilian Nuclear Deal
items.body: Democratic representatives introduced a resolution this week to block the Trump administration's new civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, PBS NewsHour reports. The agreement paves the way for the U.S. to help Saudi Arabia build a nuclear power program for peaceful purposes. Critics say it lacks sufficient safeguards and fear it could allow Saudi Arabia to pursue nuclear weapons. That is the whole argument in one sentence: whether the terms of a civilian program can be drawn tightly enough to keep a weapons capability out of reach.

sources.title: Fed Funds Expected Trajectory, and Other Rates

discussion.body: The author's interpretation is cautious: the breakeven fell, but that is not the same as declaring inflation expectations settled.
Five basis points off a five-year breakeven after a quarter-point move is barely a reaction. The expectation measure is the interesting part of that comparison.

items.title: A Quarter-Point Move, and Inflation Expectations That Haven't Quite Settled
items.body:
Econbrowser's chart of the CME FedWatch implied path has a modal prediction of another quarter-point increase in the fed funds rate by year-end. This is a market-implied prediction, not a promise of what the Federal Reserve will do.

The author also reports that the five-year inflation breakeven fell 5 basis points, while judging that a quarter-point increase had not completely quieted inflation expectations. The interesting pairing is a predicted further rate increase alongside that modest decline in the breakeven measure.

sources.title: Paradox of Hedonism

discussion.body: If an overly conscious pursuit is the problem, the way someone seeks pleasure matters. That is a more specific claim than saying every pursuit of pleasure defeats itself.
If seeking pleasure works better without focusing too hard on it, that is an odd instruction manual. A theory of what is good still leaves a practical question about how to pursue it.

items.title: The Paradox of Hedonism, and the Version of Pleasure-Seeking It Actually Targets
items.body: The paradox of hedonism holds that the pursuit of pleasure is self-defeating. Which pursuit, though, is doing the damage? The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's entry on the paradox argues that the overly conscious pursuit of pleasure, rather than the other definitions that emerge from the literature, best captures the kind of pursuit that might generate paradoxical effects. Among the competing explanations it traces, it identifies the incompetence account as the most plausible. That is a narrower target than the slogan suggests: if the trouble comes from an overly conscious pursuit of pleasure, the objection lands on a particular style of hedonism rather than on the claim that pleasure is what is good for us.

sources.title: Carney government files 3rd court challenge in First Nations child welfare complaint

items.title: Canada Challenges Another Ruling in the First Nations Child Welfare Case
items.body: The Carney government has filed its third court challenge in a year as a longstanding fight with First Nations organizations over the future of their communities' child and family services continues, CBC reports. Canada is challenging the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal's latest ruling in a case that is now nearly 20 years old. The repeated litigation is the story: a two-decade-old dispute in which the federal government is now contesting the tribunal's decisions for the third time in twelve months.

sources.title: Manitobans brace for dark mornings, lighter evenings after time change nixed

items.title: Manitoba Stops Falling Back
items.body: Manitoba's clocks will not fall back this November, Premier Wab Kinew announced Thursday, which keeps the province on daylight time through the winter rather than switching to standard time. Global News reports that mental health advocates called the end of the seasonal change a positive thing. The arithmetic of staying put is the familiar one from every debate over abolishing the switch: clocks remain an hour ahead, so winter mornings begin in deeper darkness while evenings hold their light longer. Manitoba has picked a side, at least for this November.

sources.title: Liquidity Optimization in Gross Settlement Systems with Quantum Reordering: Application to TARGET2∗

discussion.body: Promising on small batches and beaten on large ones is a division of labour, not a takeover. The interesting question is what happens as batches grow.
The machine-learning half may be the more practical part. Knowing which payment patterns can actually be improved is useful no matter which algorithm does the reordering.
Fair — the claim that survives is narrower than the exciting version: reordering helps, and how much it helps depends on batch size.

items.title: The Queue Order That Shrinks a Payment System's Liquidity Needs
items.body: In a gross settlement system, payments settle one by one, so the sequence in which queued payments go through shapes how much liquidity the system needs at any moment. A Bank of Canada paper, building on an earlier quantum algorithm, reports that reordering those queued payments can significantly reduce liquidity needs. The advantage is size-dependent: the algorithm performs well on smaller payment batches, while traditional algorithms can process larger batches and deliver greater savings. Machine learning plays a supporting role, identifying which payment patterns offer the greatest potential for improvement. Together that reads less like quantum computers replacing the plumbing than like a division of labour — the quantum method promising on small batches, classical methods still ahead on big ones, and machine learning deciding where to look.

sources.title: Hedonism

discussion.body: Including grief alongside physical discomfort makes this broader than a doctrine of indulgence. But does calling bereavement pain capture everything that matters about losing someone?

The breadth is the point rather than a bug. The theory's real bite is the denial that anything besides pleasure and pain is of ultimate importance, which is stranger than the caricature of hedonism as a doctrine of indulgence.

items.title: Hedonism Counts a Fond Memory as Pleasure and a Stubbed Toe as Pain
items.body: Hedonism's distinctive claim is not that pleasure is nice. It is that pleasure and pain are the only things of ultimate importance — a thesis that makes the theory at once simple and hard to live with. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy's examples show how broadly hedonists draw those two terms: a gentle massage and recalling a fond memory are both considered to cause pleasure, while stubbing a toe and hearing about the death of a loved one are both considered to cause pain. Once the ledger includes memory and bereavement alongside massage and stubbed toes, the doctrine stops looking like an argument for indulgence and starts looking like a claim about what is of ultimate importance.

sources.title: A new chapter for MIT Reads

items.title: MIT's Shared Reading Program Answers the AI Age With Fiction
items.body: MIT Reads, the MIT Libraries' shared reading program, is marking its 10-year anniversary by being reimagined for the age of artificial intelligence — and the reinvention points away from the technology. The program is turning its focus to fiction and memoir, and to the particular power of stories to help readers understand themselves and their place in the world. “Reading fiction prompts us to think about how what we build might change us,” says MIT Libraries Director Chris Bourg. That is a more interesting argument than the usual defence of reading as enrichment: fiction, framed this way, is where builders rehearse what their building does to them.
